nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the abolitionist writing of the free Black communities of the northern seaports, of Black mutual-aid and Masonic civic life, and of the immediatist pamphlet agitation of the later 1820s
literary_identity: Boston clothes merchant, civic organizer and pamphleteer; the author of the first and most uncompromising American demand for immediate unconditional emancipation written by a Black American, and the founding polemicist of the immediatist agitation in the United States.
biography: Walker was born in Wilmington, North Carolina, in or about 1796, and grew up free; his mother's condition and his father's status are reported differently in the sources, and under the law of the state his freedom or enslavement would have followed the condition of the mother. He appears in the record as a mariner's and then a merchant's man, with years in Charleston, South Carolina, before he settled in Boston by 1825. There he kept a clothing and second-hand goods business, joined the Prince Hall Masonic lodge and took an active part in the Black civic, mutual-aid, educational and religious networks of the city, whose print culture and subscription lists gave the abolitionist press its first readers and its earliest money. He was in sympathy with the colony scheme then advancing in the white press and became its most furious opponent, and his Appeal, issued in Boston on 28 September 1829, was printed at his own instance, smuggled into the Southern states through sailors and Black seaport channels, and reissued in three enlarged editions within a year. Its call to the enslaved to read, remember and act, and its prophecy of judgment on the republic, produced a legislative reaction in the Southern states, a bounty on his person announced in Georgia, and a permanent alarm in the slaveholding press. He died in Boston on 6 August 1830, at about thirty-four years of age, and was buried in what is now an unmarked grave; the cause of his death was never established, and from his own lifetime some suspected he had been murdered. The Liberator, founded the year after his death, printed his Appeal in full and treated it as the opening document of the movement.
literary_profile: His surviving literary work is a single pamphlet, and a work of sustained argument rather than narrative: Walker's Appeal, in four articles with a preamble, addressed in the first instance to the coloured citizens of the world and particularly of the United States. It mixes indictment, scriptural exegesis, historical parallel, statistical citation from encyclopaedias and the slave codes, and an appeal to the diaspora to educate, organise and remember itself; a supplementary appeal to the slaveholders follows in later editions. Its manner is sermon, courtroom remonstrance and open letter at once, and its four articles pass from the condition of free Black Americans, through the crimes of slavery and the rebuttal of racist pseudo-science, to a programme of self-help, schools and mutual inspection. He also wrote short public letters and minutes to the Black press of the later 1820s, and left a son of the same name who preserved the text.
stylistic_characteristics: An amplified, prophetic and incantatory prose, built on apostrophe, anaphora, long cumulative sentences and repeated charges of hypocrisy; the irony of quotation turned against the quotations' authors, with the Declaration, the Bible and the language of Christianity cited to condemn the nation that uses them. The argument proceeds by indictment, evidence and threat rather than by politeness, and it deliberately abandons the petitioning manner of earlier reform writing.
intellectual_concerns: The standing of the enslaved as fully human and as citizens of the republic that professes their equality; the sin and political danger of slavery and of the colour line; the complicity of the churches and of the colonisation movement in American slavery; the duties of self-education, industry, temperance and organisation in the free Black community; the use of scripture and of founding documents as instruments of accusation; the right of the oppressed to speak for themselves and, under judgment, to act.
historical_significance: The Appeal marks the moment when American abolitionist writing turned from gradualist appeal and white benevolence to immediate unconditional demand voiced by the oppressed themselves, and it supplied the rhetorical model of the agitation of the 1830s. It was the first American pamphlet to make the condition of the enslaved a national rather than a charitable question in the language of self-assertion; it was read aloud, reprinted, smuggled and prosecuted, and the laws passed against Black literacy and importation of seditious press in the Southern states after 1829-30 were partly a reply to it. Garrison's paper made him its prophetic precursor, and later Black radical tradition has read him as its founding political writer.
biographical_uncertainty: Almost all the facts of his life before Boston are uncertain. The year of his birth is given only approximately (c. 1796, sometimes 1797), and the date of 28 September in some accounts is borrowed from the anniversary of the Appeal's publication; the conditions of his parents, and therefore the basis of his own free status, are reported contradictorily, with one account making his mother free and his father enslaved and another the reverse. The story of his early life is derived largely from what he says of himself in the Appeal and from Southern newspaper reportage hostile to him. The cause of his death is unknown, and the poisoning theory belongs to contemporary suspicion and to later tradition rather than to evidence. No manuscript of the Appeal survives and the details of its printing and distribution are known from the editions themselves and from the reports of agents.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the Quaker plain-style remonstrance, the women's anti-slavery agitation of the Midlands, and British immediatism
literary_identity: Leicester banker's wife, plain-style Quaker and pamphleteer; the writer of the tract which broke the British movement's long gradualism and supplied the slogan and the logic of immediate emancipation.
biography: Heyrick was born Elizabeth Coltman at Leicester on 4 December 1769, the daughter of John Coltman, a surgeon and apothecary of the town, and was educated in a family of dissenting and then Quaker connection. She married John Heyrick, a Leicester banker and businessman whose affairs miscarried, and after his death and the failure of the house she maintained herself and her daughters in the town by keeping a shop and by her writings, living a life of plain-living, careful dressing of the poor and strenuous correspondence. She joined the Society of Friends, and her Quaker habits of remonstrance, of the plain style and of personal testimony shaped everything she printed. She had long written against the slave trade and the colonies, sending tracts on the subject to Zachary Macaulay and to the friends of gradual measure, and in 1824 she threw a printed circular, Immediate, Not Gradual Abolition, upon the members of the London society, following it with an Apologia and with the arguments addressed to the conscience of the slave-holder and to the West India interest. The pamphlet was passed from hand to hand, reprinted, and made the turning-point of the agitation, furnishing the demand for unconditional and immediate emancipation which the new society of 1831 adopted and which the abolition act of 1833 carried. She was one of the first to urge the women's anti-slavery societies, the boycott of slave-grown sugar and the apprenticeship scheme's rejection, and she corresponded with American friends on the colonisation enterprise, denouncing the American Colonization Society in letters published after her death. She died at Leicester on 18 October 1831, within a few months of the foundation of the society which took her programme, and her posthumous volume of essays and letters on the colonies appeared in 1832.
literary_profile: Her writing is the short reform tract and the printed circular, argumentative, urgent and addressed to a named society or to the reader's conscience: the 1824 pamphlet states the case for the shortest, safest and most effectual means of getting rid of colonial slavery, and the Apologia of 1825 defends the principle against the gradualists of her own party. Her later letters on the colonisation system and her essays on the condition of the people, published in a volume after her death, extend the same method of plain appeal, arithmetic and moral demonstration. She wrote also on war and nonresistance, on the treatment of animals and on the education and dress of the labouring poor, in a literature of remonstrance rather than of system.
stylistic_characteristics: The plain Quaker style of remonstrance: direct address, short declarative sentences, the pointed question, the enumeration of instances and the arithmetic of compensation turned against the claim it supports; an absence of ornament and of classical allusion, and a moral pressure carried by repetition and by the refusal of euphemism. The tone is neither petitioning nor declamatory but adjuring, and it is frequently startling because it will not concede the premises of its opponents.
intellectual_concerns: The sin of holding the enslaved and the impossibility of a just gradual measure; immediate emancipation without compensation to the holder; the duty of the consumer, and the boycott of the product of slave labour; the claims of women to take a public part in moral agitation; nonresistance, the cruelty of war and the treatment of animals and of the poor as one question of justice; the colonisation of free Black Americans as a scheme of expulsion rather than of liberation.
historical_significance: Her pamphlet is the pivot text of British immediatism, the document that shifted the agitations demand from apprenticeship and gradual measure to unconditional emancipation, and it directly shaped the programme of the society founded in 1831 and the argument over compensation before the legislation of 1833. She is also a founding figure of women's organised anti-slavery work in England, since her circulars and her example supplied the logic of the female societies and of the sugar boycott, and her colonisation letters carried into the American debate.
biographical_uncertainty: Her birth and death dates are given in the parish and family records of Leicester but are omitted altogether, or printed wrongly, in many standard histories of the movement and in most nineteenth-century notices, and her place of birth is sometimes stated only as the town, sometimes as a village near it. The extent of her authorship of anonymous tracts and letters in the abolitionist press is uncertain, and the part she played in the founding of the Leicester ladies society and in the national immediate-abolition organisation of 1830-31 is known chiefly from the proceedings and the correspondence of those bodies.

alternative_names: The founder of the abolition committee
nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the abolitionist movement and its literature, and the reform writing of the Atlantic world
literary_identity: Scholar, investigator, organiser and historian of the abolition movement; the man who turned a college essay question into a quarter-century of evidence-gathering, travel and publication, and who wrote the movement's first and greatest documentary history.
biography: Clarkson was born at Wisbech in Cambridgeshire on 28 March 1760, the son of the headmaster of the free grammar school of the town, a clergyman who died while Thomas was still a child, and he was brought up in a family of some letters and small means. He went to St John's College, Cambridge, took his degrees, won the university's Latin prize in 1785 for an essay on the slavery and commerce of the human species, and found in the reading of that essay the conviction that fixed his life. He removed to London, where the Latin essay, translated and published in 1786, brought him into acquaintance with the Quaker friends of the cause and with Granville Sharp, and in 1787 he was a founding member of the committee of the Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade. For the next twenty years he made the movement's evidence: he travelled some thirty-five thousand miles to the seaports and the great trading towns, collected the ships' papers, the cargoes, the surgeons' depositions and the testimony of sailors and of the enslaved themselves, drew up the plans and the sections of a slave ship which became the movement's most famous image, and wrote the pamphlets, the summaries and the appeals that carried the case to the counties and to Parliament. He was the chief labourer of a campaign in which others spoke in the House, and he saw the abolition of the trade carried in 1807. He settled in 1816 at Playford in Suffolk, where he passed his last years in retired literary, religious and agricultural work; the great History of the Rise, Progress, and Accomplishment of the Abolition of the African Slave-Trade by the British Parliament appeared in 1808, followed later by a portrait of the system of colonial slavery and by tracts on moral and religious improvement; his own life, begun for publication, was finished after his death by his daughter. He died at Playford on 26 September 1846, the last survivor of the founding committee, and was buried in the churchyard there, with a commemoration in Westminster Abbey raised by the subscribers of the cause.
literary_profile: His writings form a deliberate literature of evidence and of argument: the Latin dissertation and its English translation state the moral and classical case against slavery; the Essay on the Slave Trade, the Summary View and the addresses to the people of England, to the legislators and to the merchants press the argument by fact; the History of 1808, in two volumes, is at once a personal narrative of the agitation, a documentary record of the trade and an argumentative history of a quarter-century of public work. He wrote also on the African commerce and the colonies, on the condition of the enslaved in the colonies, on rural economy and on his own parish, and his letters and his unfinished autobiography belong to the same body of reform life-writing.
stylistic_characteristics: A plain, earnest and cumulative prose of enquiry, in which the argument is carried by enumeration, by the deposition and by the specification of fact rather than by rhetoric, and by a persistent moral address to the reader's humanity; the long sentence of the eighteenth-century argumentative style, with little ornament and a frequent appeal to scripture, to law and to common observation. In the History the manner becomes at once judicial and personal, the investigator's record interwoven with the narrative of his own journeys and labour.
intellectual_concerns: The evidence for the cruelty and the waste of the trade, and the duty of enquiry and of publication; the relation of testimony, document and image to moral argument; the obligations of the Christian and commercial nation to its own conduct; the education and the improvement of the labouring poor and of the African; the claims of humanity toward animals and toward the colonised; the history and the morality of a successful agitation, and the example it offers to future reform.
historical_significance: He made the British abolition movement into an organised public enquiry, and the evidence he gathered, the plans he caused to be drawn and the pamphlets he wrote gave the cause the documents on which its parliamentary success depended; the act of 1807 was in great part the result of his labour. His History of 1808 is the foundational documentary history of the movement and one of the largest works of argumentative prose in the reform literature of the period, and his method of accumulated testimony became the model on which later agitations, American as well as British, were conducted.
biographical_uncertainty: The details of his collections and of the priority of the several plans, images and depots of evidence used by the society are difficult to disentangle, since the committee's papers and its published accounts do not always mark authorship; the date and place of his retirement residence are given variously before his settlement at Playford, and the text of his autobiography, begun by himself and completed and edited after his death by his daughter, cannot be wholly separated from her hand.

birthplace: Baa, on the West African coast (the African name and the place as given in his own narrative; the modern identification is disputed)
nationality_or_literary_tradition: American (born in West Africa); the earliest Afro-American slave narrative and the life-writing of the free Black communities of New England
literary_identity: A man born in Africa, enslaved in Rhode Island and Connecticut, who purchased his own freedom and that of his family and dictated the earliest secular slave narrative printed in the United States; the author-assert, in his own first person, of an African past, of the Middle Passage and of a lifetime of labour, contract and lawsuit.
biography: He was born Broteer Furro, as he said, the eldest son of a ruler in an African country on the coast known to him as Baa, and was taken in a raid on his father's town when he was a boy of about sixteen, marched to the coast and sold; the year and the place of his birth he gave only as his memory and his account could give them. He was carried across the Atlantic, passed through the markets of the West Indies and was sold at Newport in the Rhode Island colony; he took the name Venture from an English word written on papers of his purchase, and the surname Smith from his last Connecticut owner, and he passed through several New England masters, serving in households, on the water and in the labour of the seaport towns. By the labour of many years, by contracts of hire he kept to the letter, and by the help of friends among the free Black people and the white neighbours of the Connecticut coast, he bought his own freedom at New London in 1746 and afterwards the freedom of his wife Meg and of his children, paying the prices and recording them. He worked as a mariner, a farm labourer, a woodcutter and a small proprietor, saved money, bought land, and in his later years lived at Haddam in Connecticut as a free landholder and parent of a considerable family, pursuing in the courts a man who had illegally sold his wife and recovering something of the loss. In his seventies he caused the history of his life to be drawn up and published at New London in 1798, taken down from his own mouth by a local compiler, and the volume sets out the African succession and politics of his father's country, the manner of his capture, the voyage, the slave markets of the West Indies and of the northern colonies, and the exact sums of his earnings and purchases. He died in 1805 at Haddam and was buried in the graveyard of the church at East Haddam, where his headstone, raised long afterward by his descendants and by the historical society, records the dates he gave him.
literary_profile: His Narrative is a short first-person life taken down from his mouth and printed as related by himself, and it divides between the African chapters, an account of the country, the succession and the raid that ended his childhood which has no parallel in the later genre, the Middle Passage and the sale, and the long American record of labour, wages, contracts, prices paid and lawsuits. The economic detail is its distinguishing feature: the sums earned and paid, the terms of hire, the cost of his own and his family's freedom, and the final pursuit of the man who sold his wife are set down with a specificity absent from the religious narratives that followed. It is autobiography and evidence at once, and it closes with the facts of his property and his family.
stylistic_characteristics: A flat, concrete and unsentimental narrative voice, in the first person and without appeal to the reader's pity, resting on date, place, name and amount; the phrase of the account rendered rather than of the complaint made. The compiler's literary hand is visible in the framing and in the moralising touches, but the matter and the manner of counting are his own, and the effect of plain statement is the more powerful for the absence of rhetoric.
intellectual_concerns: The fact of an African history, name and family before enslavement; the actual conduct of the trade from the coast through the voyage to the market; the meaning of freedom as the power to earn, to contract, to buy persons out of slavery and to hold land; the law as an instrument available, however imperfectly, to a free Black man; the worth of labour and the record of its price; the duty of a father and a husband in a condition that denied both.
historical_significance: His narrative is the earliest secular slave narrative printed in the United States and one of the strongest surviving first-person accounts of African origins, the Middle Passage and the slave markets of the northern colonies and the West Indies; it antedates and differs from the religious confession-model that hardened in the genre. Its records are used as primary evidence for the trade, for the labor and wages of enslaved and free Black people in New England, and for the founding of a free Black propertied community, and it stands at the origin of the Afro-American autobiography.
biographical_uncertainty: His birth year and his African origin are self-reported and approximate: the narrative gives the place as Baa and the country of his father's rule in his own terms, and modern scholars have placed it variously in what are now Nigeria, Ghana and Guinea, with the date of his birth estimated at about 1729 from his account of his age at capture, while older editions and notices put it nearer 1700. His African name, his age, the dates of his sale and of his several transfers, and the details of the lawsuit for his wife come only from the dictated narrative and from such local records as survive, and the compiler's share of the composition cannot be measured. The date of his death and the inscription of the gravestone are recorded in Haddam and East Haddam sources and in the family account.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the Garrisonian reform press of Boston and the immediatist abolitionist movement
literary_identity: Journalist, editor and agitator; the founder and editor of The Liberator and the chief architect of American immediate-emancipation doctrine, of the reform newspaper as an instrument of mass moral agitation, and of the moral-suasion wing of the movement.
biography: Garrison was born at Newburyport, Massachusetts, on 10 December 1805, the son of a sailing captain of difficult circumstances who emigrated to Europe and died abroad, and he grew up in partial want. He was apprenticed as a boy to a Newburyport printer, worked in Boston composing rooms, and by his early twenties was printing and editing on his own account; he took up the temperance cause, protested the treatment of seamen, and was at first friendly to the colonisation enterprise. He became agent for the American Colonization Society in 1828, but the friendship of Benjamin Lundy and his growing conviction that the society was a plan for expelling rather than freeing the enslaved turned him to immediate emancipation. On 1 January 1831 he began The Liberator in Boston with the famous resolution not to equivocate, not to retreat and to be heard, and it ran weekly for thirty-four years to 1865. The New England Anti-Slavery Society followed in 1832, the American Anti-Slavery Society in 1833, and the movement's mail, its meeting-house and its agent's lives were attacked: a mob tried to seize him in 1835 and the post office excluded abolitionist matter from Southern delivery. His principles widened into a general reform programme of nonresistance, women's rights and moral suasion, and he broke with the political abolitionists and with most of his former allies in 1840 over the participation of women and over his refusal of voting and office-holding as support for a slaveholding constitution. The disunion slogan of the 1840s and his public burning of the Fugitive Slave Law and of a pro-slavery sermon in the 1850s expressed the same logic; the Thirteenth Amendment and the end of slavery in 1865 allowed him to close the Liberator. He lived his last years in Boston, engaged in women's suffrage, education and prison and labour reform, and died in New York on 24 May 1879 at his daughter's house. He left behind the movement he founded and the model of the reform editor who makes a weekly paper into a book of argument.
literary_profile: His literary medium was the periodical: four thousand weekly numbers of The Liberator, with its leading articles, its reprinted testimony, its correspondence, its poetry and its documentary appendix, together with the open letters to public men, the remonstrances to legislatures, the 1832 tract on the colonisation society, and the speeches of his two lecture tours in Britain. He wrote also pamphlets of doctrine on the character of the federal compact as an agreement with slavery, and a large body of correspondence which is itself part of the movement's literature. His editorial practice is itself a literary achievement: he built a paper out of letters, testimony, and reprinting, and made the aggregate of documents into argument.
stylistic_characteristics: A plain New England prose of high moral pressure, in which short declarative sentences and anaphora of resolution give way to long periods of indictment; directness deliberately courted, with the plain style of Quaker remonstrance fused to the jeremiad and to the revival address. The prose shifts between the editorial we, the first-person vow and the second-person arraigning of the reader, and it is unreservedly figurative, turning on the language of blood, compact, altar and judgment.
intellectual_concerns: Immediate and unconditional emancipation without compensation; the Constitution and the churches as compacts with slavery; moral suasion as the means of reform against political and clerical management; the identity of the slave's cause with the freedom of speech and of the press; the rights of women as inseparable from the rights of the enslaved; nonresistance, pacifism and the refusal of oaths and office; the brotherhood of humanity and the sin of colonisation and of prejudice.
historical_significance: Garrison converted American abolition from a charitable and gradualist project into a mass movement with its own vocabulary, its own press and its own full-time agents, and The Liberator remains the model of the reform periodical that makes an agitation. His intransigent rhetoric, and his willingness to be hated, made slavery a national question of conscience rather than of policy, and his quarrels over politics, women and the Constitution shaped the party and clerical lines of the movement for thirty years. He is the central figure of the sectional literature of the 1830s and 1840s and a defining instance of the Romantic reform writer whose paper is his book.
biographical_uncertainty: The day of his birth is given as 10 December 1805 in most accounts and as 12 December in some official biographical notes. The details of his apprenticeships and of the first years of his own printing and editing are recorded mainly from his own later reminiscence and from the memories of associates, and the chronology of his conversion from colonisation agency to immediatism in 1828-29 is variously assigned between the influence of Lundy, his own reading and his quarrel with society managers. His authorship of unsigned leading articles in his own paper is a matter of editorial convention rather than of itemised record.
